title: Complexity of Rotation Distance Between Binary Search Trees
statement_text: What is the computational complexity of computing the rotation distance between two binary search trees (equivalently, the flip distance between two triangulations of a convex polygon)?
context_text: A rotation in a binary search tree is the local restructuring operation that makes a child the parent of its former parent while preserving the in-order of the keys; the rotation distance between two binary search trees on the same keys is the minimum number of rotations transforming one into the other. Via the classical Catalan bijection mapping a triangulation of a convex polygon to its dual tree, this equals the flip distance between triangulations, where a flip replaces the diagonal of a quadrilateral formed by two adjacent triangles by the other diagonal; equivalently, it is the distance between two vertices on the skeleton (graph of vertices and edges) of the associahedron. The authors stress that the complexity status of this problem is widely open: it is not known to be NP-hard, but no polynomial-time algorithm is known either; only a simple polynomial-time 2-approximation and several fixed-parameter algorithms are known. In contrast, flip distances between triangulations of arbitrary point sets or polygons are NP-hard. This is one of the main motivations of the paper, which proves that computing shortest paths on the skeleton of polymatroids (generalized permutohedra, of which associahedra are examples) is NP-hard, even for very simple polymatroids in $\mathbb{R}^n$ defined by $O(n)$ inequalities, and hard to approximate when the polymatroid is given by a submodular-function oracle.

title: Complexity of Flip Distance Between Rectangulations
statement_text: What is the computational complexity of computing the flip distance between two rectangulations of a unit square?
context_text: A rectangulation is a tessellation of the unit square into disjoint axis-aligned rectangles; modulo a natural equivalence, rectangulations are in bijection with classes of pattern-avoiding permutations. As for triangulations, flip graphs on rectangulations can be defined, and they are skeletons (graphs of vertices and edges) of polytopes; the flip distance between two rectangulations is their distance in this flip graph. These polytopes belong to the family of quotientopes and are polymatroids (generalized permutohedra), so computing flip distances between rectangulations is a special case of computing shortest paths on the skeleton of a polymatroid. The authors prove that the latter is NP-hard in general, even for very simple polymatroids defined by $O(n)$ inequalities, but state that the complexity of the flip distance problems between rectangulations is open (as is, famously, the rotation distance between binary search trees, i.e. flip distance on the associahedron).
